Anthropic staff and US workers don’t seem to have different theories about how AI affects jobs. Instead, they have different experiences of what AI capabilities are. Those different experiences seem closely related to perceptions about what will happen to work in the future. Anthropic is a company at the frontier of AI adoption, and that adoption has changed the way we hire. We find that over the past year, we're hiring for a smaller share of junior positions, and a smaller share of our employees work in technical roles. At the same time, the rate of hours worked by AI agents has shot up. By March 2026, agents worked more hours than employees. By August, there were six times more agents than employees at Anthropic, and productivity increased. That’s led to Anthropic producing more code per person, but that’s a notoriously imperfect measure. We see signs of increased productivity elsewhere: we’ve closed more sales per sales representative, and processed more contracts. When our researchers follow the same employee over time, they find the employee’s output rises as their adoption of AI tools increases. candidates.title: How employment is changing at Anthropic
candidates.summary: Economics How employment is changing at Anthropic Oct 16, 2026 Read in PDF Nathan Wilmers, Regina Catipon, Maxim Massenkoff, Peter McCrory How has AI restructured work and employment at Anthropic? As a company at the frontier of AI adoption, Anthropic could be a leading indicator of how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy. Key findings Anthropic has been hiring for a smaller share of junior technical positions. This occurred as hours worked by AI agents relative to employees rapidly expanded. By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees’ six to one. As AI agents diffused through the company, Anthropic began producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts. Following the same employee over time, output rose as they adopted new AI tools. This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines. Changes in work organization are reflected in shifting priorities among hiring managers, who increasingly emphasize autonomy and judgment, relative to technical domain expertise and implementation. candidates.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
candidates.summary: Science Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude Oct 16, 2026 Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated. This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv . Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. candidates.title: The AI expectations gap
candidates.summary: Economics The AI expectations gap Oct 16, 2026 Read in PDF Szymon Sacher, Tess Cotter, Charles I. Jones, Anton Korinek, Peter McCrory Key findings US adults expect AI capabilities to advance rapidly in the coming years; Anthropic staff expect even faster progress; 39% of US adults and 91% of staff expect that AI will be able to make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030. Anthropic staff expect much larger productivity gains from AI on the tasks it is well-suited for. Among US adults who use AI at work, 26% say a task takes a quarter of the time or less with AI, compared to 59% of Anthropic staff. When it comes to their own job, over half of Anthropic staff expect AI to be able to do at least 80% of their current work by 2030, compared with 5% of US workers. Among both US workers and Anthropic staff, people who expect AI to do more of their own work anticipate higher unemployment. While there are differences in beliefs about future capabilities, the perceived link between how AI might change one’s own job and broader unemployment is very similar for both groups. Introduction How will AI reshape the economy in the years ahead? AI capabilities are advancing rapidly, and the possibility that future AI models may be able to build their own successors (recursive self-improvement) could further accelerate the rate of progress. candidates.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
candidates.summary: Frontier Red Team Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins Oct 16, 2026 “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained. We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards. Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy. ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from.
